GPS vs Phone Navigation for Motorcycle Touring

Navigation is essential for motorcycle touring, but the choice between a dedicated GPS unit and your smartphone isn't as clear-cut as it once was. Both have evolved significantly, and both have real strengths and weaknesses for UK riding.

Dedicated GPS Units

Devices like the Garmin Zumo and TomTom Rider are purpose-built for motorcycle navigation.

Advantages:

  • Built for the environment: Waterproof, vibration-resistant, glove-friendly touchscreens. These are designed to be on a motorcycle, not in a pocket.
  • Sunlight-readable screens: Transflective displays are visible in direct sunlight without draining battery.
  • Motorcycle-specific routing: Many GPS units offer "curvy road" routing that prioritises interesting roads over the fastest route. This is gold for touring.
  • No phone damage: Motorcycle vibrations can damage phone camera stabilisation systems. Using a dedicated GPS keeps your phone safe in your pocket.
  • Battery independence: Your phone battery stays full for photos, calls, and emergencies.

Disadvantages:

  • Cost: £250-500 for a quality motorcycle GPS
  • Map updates can be slow or require a computer
  • Another device to charge, mount, and maintain
  • Less intuitive than phone apps for many riders

Smartphone Navigation

Apps like Google Maps, Waze, Calimoto, and Kurviger have made phone navigation incredibly capable.

Advantages:

  • You already own one: No additional cost beyond a mount and possibly a case.
  • Always-current maps: App updates are automatic and free.
  • Versatility: Music, photos, calls, and navigation on one device.
  • Route sharing: Easily share routes with other riders via WhatsApp, email, or social media.
  • Community features: Apps like Calimoto have rider communities sharing routes and ratings.

Disadvantages:

  • Vibration damage: Apple has warned that motorcycle vibrations can damage iPhone camera systems. This is a documented, real problem. Consider a vibration-dampening mount.
  • Screen visibility: Phone screens wash out in direct sunlight. Anti-glare screen protectors help but don't solve it completely.
  • Battery drain: Running GPS with screen on drains batteries fast. You'll need a 12V USB power supply wired to your bike.
  • Weather vulnerability: Most phones aren't truly waterproof under sustained rain. A waterproof case is essential.
Our recommendation for UK touring: use a phone as your primary navigation device with a vibration-dampening mount, waterproof case, and wired power supply. Download offline maps for your route area. Keep a paper map as backup. If budget allows, a dedicated GPS is the premium choice.

Essential Apps for UK Motorcycle Navigation

  • OS Maps: The gold standard for UK mapping. Offline maps available. Shows terrain, paths, and detail no other app matches.
  • Google Maps: Good for general navigation and finding services (fuel, food, accommodation).
  • Calimoto: Motorcycle-specific routing that favours twisty roads. Has a good UK road database.
  • Kurviger: Excellent for planning curvy motorcycle routes. Avoids motorways by default.
  • What3Words: Useful for communicating exact locations in emergencies — used by UK emergency services.

Offline Maps: Non-Negotiable for UK Touring

Mobile signal in rural Britain is patchy at best and non-existent in many touring areas. Always download offline maps before you set off:

  • Download the full area you'll be touring through, not just your planned route
  • Google Maps, OS Maps, and Kurviger all support offline map downloads
  • Test offline navigation before departure — some features behave differently offline
  • Offline maps can be 500MB-2GB depending on area size, so manage your phone storage

Whatever you choose, the key is testing your setup thoroughly before your tour. A navigation system you don't trust is worse than no navigation at all — you'll spend more time worrying about it than enjoying the road. faq.q: Is a dedicated GPS better than a phone for touring?
faq.a: Each has strengths. A dedicated GPS such as the Garmin Zumo or TomTom Rider is waterproof, vibration-resistant, readable in sunlight and offers curvy-road routing, but costs £250 to £500. A phone costs nothing extra beyond a mount and has free, always-current maps. Our UK recommendation is a phone as primary with a dedicated GPS as the premium choice if budget allows.

faq.q: Can a motorcycle really damage my phone?
faq.a: Yes. Apple has warned that motorcycle vibrations can damage iPhone camera systems, and this is a documented, real problem. Use a vibration-dampening mount to reduce the risk. Using a dedicated GPS instead keeps your phone safe in your pocket and preserves its battery for photos, calls and emergencies.

faq.q: What is the recommended UK navigation setup?
faq.a: Use a phone as your primary navigation device with a vibration-dampening mount, a waterproof case and a wired 12V power supply, and download offline maps for your route area. Keep a paper map as backup. If budget allows, add a dedicated motorcycle GPS as the premium option for its sunlight-readable screen and rugged build.

faq.q: Which apps are best for UK motorcycle navigation?
faq.a: OS Maps is the gold standard for UK mapping with unmatched terrain detail and offline maps. Google Maps is good for general navigation and finding fuel, food and accommodation. Calimoto and Kurviger both favour twisty roads and avoid motorways, and What3Words helps communicate exact locations to UK emergency services.

faq.q: Why are offline maps so important?
faq.a: Mobile signal in rural Britain is patchy at best and non-existent in many touring areas, so downloading offline maps before you set off is non-negotiable. Download the full area you will tour through, not just your route, test offline navigation before departure, and remember offline maps can be 500MB to 2GB, so manage your phone storage.
